### Developer Tooling

Additional scripts for day-to-day development — auto-fix, watch mode, and an interactive CLI.

#### `scripts/validate-autofix.py` — detect and auto-fix routing errors

Detects and optionally fixes 3 common routing error classes:

| Error class | Detected | Auto-fixed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Missing alias in `aliases.yaml` | ✅ | ✅ |
| Incorrect agent ID in `matrix.yaml` | ✅ | ✅ |
| Orphaned prompt reference in `matrix.yaml` | ✅ | ✅ |

```bash
# Detect only (safe, no writes)
./.venv/bin/python scripts/validate-autofix.py

# Detect and fix in place
./.venv/bin/python scripts/validate-autofix.py --fix

# Generate a Markdown report (written to reports/)
./.venv/bin/python scripts/validate-autofix.py --report --report-format markdown

# Generate a JSON report for CI artifact upload
./.venv/bin/python scripts/validate-autofix.py --report --report-format json
```

#### `scripts/validate-watch.py` — continuous validation on file change

Polls `routing/` and `.github/` directories and reruns validators automatically on any change. Validation cycle is under 2 seconds.

```bash
# Watch mode (runs indefinitely)
./.venv/bin/python scripts/validate-watch.py

# Single run (CI-friendly, exits after one pass)
./.venv/bin/python scripts/validate-watch.py --once

# Watch only specific validators
./.venv/bin/python scripts/validate-watch.py --validators smoke autofix
```

#### `scripts/install-hooks.py` — install pre-commit hooks

Installs the scope-filtered pre-commit hook from `scripts/hooks/pre-commit` into `.git/hooks/`. The hook runs validators only when routing or `.github/` files are staged.

```bash
# Install the pre-commit hook
./.venv/bin/python scripts/install-hooks.py

# Check if hooks are installed (no writes)
./.venv/bin/python scripts/install-hooks.py --check
```

#### `scripts/codev-dev.py` — interactive developer CLI

Guide contributors through route selection, issue drafting, test-plan drafting,
PR checklist preparation, routing exploration, agent scaffolding, and
repository health checks.

| Command | Description | Writes files? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `test-route "<phrase>"` | Show routing result for any phrase with rationale | Never |
| `guide route "<request>"` | Preview whether `/route` or `/quickstart` is the right next step | Never |
| `guide extension --kind <kind>` | Preview the shortest extension onboarding path and validators | Never |
| `guide issue --title ... --summary ...` | Preview a governance-compliant issue body | Never |
| `guide test-plan --what ... --why ...` | Preview a test-plan block with CI gate | Never |
| `guide pr-checklist --issue N` | Preview a PR checklist body | Never |
| `doctor` | Check required files and run all validators | Never |
| `new agent <name>` | Scaffold a new agent file (dry-run by default) | Only with `--write` |

```bash
# Preview the next routing move without touching files
./.venv/bin/python scripts/codev-dev.py guide route "debug kubernetes pod"

# Preview the shortest extension onboarding path
./.venv/bin/python scripts/codev-dev.py guide extension --kind agent

# Preview an issue body before opening GitHub
./.venv/bin/python scripts/codev-dev.py guide issue --title "Add guided CLI flow" --summary "Help contributors prepare issue bodies"

# Route any phrase interactively
./.venv/bin/python scripts/codev-dev.py test-route "debug kubernetes pod"

# List all known routing aliases grouped by capability
./.venv/bin/python scripts/codev-dev.py test-route --list

# Run repository health check
./.venv/bin/python scripts/codev-dev.py doctor

# Scaffold a new agent (dry-run — prints output, writes nothing)
./.venv/bin/python scripts/codev-dev.py new agent my-agent

# Scaffold and write to .github/agents/ (requires --write)
./.venv/bin/python scripts/codev-dev.py new agent my-agent --write
```

> **Safety contract**: `test-route`, `guide`, and `doctor` are 100% read-only. `new agent` dry-runs by default and never overwrites an existing file.

See [docs/codev-dev-guide.md](docs/codev-dev-guide.md) for persona walkthroughs, step-count measurements, and doctor verification results.

## Routing System

The routing system is defined in four YAML files under `routing/`:

These inventories are generated from the routing source files so the README stays aligned with the
actual matrix.

### `routing/capabilities.yaml`

Defines **what** Copilot can do. Each capability has an `id` and a `default_agent`.

<!-- codev:generated:capabilities:start -->
| Capability ID | Description | Default Agent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `routing` | Route a request using the canonical capability + domain matrix. | Router |
| `debugging` | Bug triage, reproduction, instrumentation, root cause analysis. | Reliability |
| `postmortem` | Incident analysis, timeline, RCA, action items (blameless). | Reliability |
| `code-analysis` | Explain code, identify flows/invariants, generate doc-ready explanations. | Architect |
| `docs` | Generate repository and reference documentation. | Delivery Lead |
| `docs-system` | Doc architecture model, markdown standards, linting, doc governance. | Delivery Lead |
| `testing-quality` | Test planning, writing tests, quality gates, linters. | Architect |

# Login Anomaly Scorer (Impossible-Travel & Device-Mismatch)

Detects unusual sign-in behaviour (e.g., impossible travel, device/UA switches, first-seen networks) and writes a ranked `alerts.csv` for triage. Optional anomaly ranking adds a lightweight ML signal (Isolation Forest).

---

## Project layout (modular `src` style)

repo_root/
- README.md
- requirements.txt
- .gitignore
- data/                 # generated files live here
- src/
  - login_scorer/
    - __init__.py
    - data_gen.py       # synthetic data generator
    - features.py       # feature/signal engineering
    - rules.py          # rule-based scoring + reasons
    - iforest.py        # optional IsolationForest anomaly score
    - cli.py            # CLI entrypoint

---

## Install

**Windows**
1) Create venv: `python -m venv .venv`
2) Activate: `.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1`
3) Upgrade pip: `pip install --upgrade pip`
4) Install deps: `pip install -r requirements.txt`

**macOS / Linux**
1) Create venv: `python -m venv .venv`
2) Activate: `source .venv/bin/activate`
3) Upgrade pip: `pip install --upgrade pip`
4) Install deps: `pip install -r requirements.txt`

---

## How to run

1) Generate synthetic sign-ins: `python -m src.login_scorer.cli --gen` → writes `data/sample_logins.csv`

2) Score with rules (impossible travel, device/UA change, rare ASN): `python -m src.login_scorer.cli` → writes `data/alerts.csv` (adds `score`, `reason`)

3) Optional: add ML anomaly ranking (Isolation Forest): `python -m src.login_scorer.cli --iforest` → rewrites `data/alerts.csv` adding `iforest_score`, prints precision@10 if labels exist

### CLI options
- `--gen` (boolean): create synthetic input at `data/sample_logins.csv`
- `--iforest` (boolean): add Isolation Forest anomaly ranking
- `--in_csv PATH` (string): input CSV path (default `data/sample_logins.csv`)
- `--out_csv PATH` (string): output CSV path (default `data/alerts.csv`)
- `--max_speed FLOAT` (default 900.0): impossible-travel threshold in km/h
- `--sortby` {score,iforest_score} (default score): column used to sort preview/CSV
- `--top INT` (default 10): how many rows to preview in terminal

Examples:
- Rules only, default threshold:  
  `python -m src.login_scorer.cli`
- Stricter speed threshold:  
  `python -m src.login_scorer.cli --max_speed 700`
- Add ML and keep rules primary (IF acts as a tiebreaker inside the same rule score):  
  `python -m src.login_scorer.cli --iforest`
- Sort primarily by ML (demo):  
  `python -m src.login_scorer.cli --iforest --sortby iforest_score --top 15`


## What it computes (features)

- `km` — great-circle distance to the previous login for the same user
- `mins` — minutes since the previous login
- `kmph` — speed (km/h) = `km / mins * 60`
- `ua_changed` — 1 if User-Agent (browser/OS) changed since previous login
- `dev_changed` — 1 if device ID changed
- `asn_rare` — 1 if this ASN (network/ISP) is first-seen for the user

Notes: ASN = Autonomous System Number (network owner of an IP); UA = User-Agent (browser/OS string); lat/lon are synthetic (sampled from a small city list).

---

## Scoring (rules)

- Impossible travel: `kmph > 900` → +2 points (tag `impossible_travel`)
- Device/UA change: either changed → +1 point (tag `device_mismatch`)
- Rare ASN: first-seen for user → +1 point (tag `rare_asn`)
- Sum → `score` (higher = more suspicious)
- `reason` lists the rule tags (e.g., `impossible_travel;device_mismatch`)

**Sorting behaviour:** keep rules primary. With `--iforest`, the pipeline sorts by `score` and uses `iforest_score` as a **tiebreaker** among rows with the same rule score. (You can override with `--sortby iforest_score` for demo purposes.)

---

## Optional anomaly ranking (ML)

Adds `iforest_score` via Isolation Forest (unsupervised outlier detection). Use it as a secondary ranking signal (e.g., sort by `score` then by `iforest_score` to break ties). Rules remain primary for explainability.

---

## Reproducibility

To get the same synthetic data every run, set a fixed seed at the top of `data_gen.py`:
`import random, numpy as np` then `random.seed(42); np.random.seed(42)`.

---

## Outputs

- `data/sample_logins.csv` — synthetic sign-ins (created by `--gen`)
- `data/alerts.csv` — scored results (`score`, `reason`, optional `iforest_score`)

---

## Typical workflow

1) Generate a dataset (`--gen`)
2) Score with rules (and optionally using `--iforest`)
3) Open `data/alerts.csv` and review the top rows by `score` (and `iforest_score`)

---

## Limitations & next steps

- VPNs/shared IPs can create false positives (geo/ASN can be misleading)
- Next: time-of-day per-user baselines, country allow-lists, IP reputation, session binding
- In production, geo/ASN come from real enrichment, not synthetic values

# Log Anomaly Detection Decision System

## 1. Executive Summary

This repository implements an **offline, reproducible log anomaly detection system** for NASA-style HTTP access logs. It combines **time-aware feature engineering**, **multiple unsupervised detectors** (Isolation Forest baseline plus Local Outlier Factor and One-Class SVM), **controlled synthetic anomaly injection** for **valid supervised evaluation**, and a **configurable decision layer** that maps scores to `ignore` / `investigate` / `alert`. Outputs are structured for triage: per-request scores, an alert rollup, and a JSON evaluation report with **honest** precision/recall/F1 against injected labels only.

## 2. Problem

Web and application logs are high-volume, mostly normal, and occasionally contain traffic that is **abnormal** relative to typical behavior (bursts, rare status codes, odd URLs, coordinated timing). Operators need:

- A **score** that ranks suspicious lines.
- A **decision** that maps scores to operational handling without pretending unsupervised models have oracle labels on real traffic.
- **Evaluation** that is **defensible**: metrics tied to **known** synthetic anomalies, not fabricated all-normal ground truth.

## 3. System Overview

End-to-end flow:

**Data → preprocess → time split → synthetic injection (eval only) → feature engineering → scale → fit models → score → evaluate vs injection labels → apply decision thresholds → write artifacts.**

| Stage | Location |
|--------|----------|
| Load / clean / time parse | `pipeline/load_data.py`, `pipeline/preprocess.py` |
| Injection (labeled) | `evaluation/inject.py` |
| Features | `pipeline/features.py` |
| Models + scaling | `models/detector.py` |
| Metrics + threshold sweep | `evaluation/metrics.py`, `evaluation/thresholds.py` |
| Decisions | `decision_engine/engine.py` |
| Orchestration | `pipeline/orchestrator.py` |
| Entrypoint | `run.py` |
| Configuration | `configs/default.yaml`, `configs/smoke.yaml` |

Run everything with:

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
python run.py --config configs/default.yaml
```

For a **fast** reproducible check on a small slice:

```bash
python run.py --config configs/smoke.yaml
```

## 4. Data & Anomaly Injection

- **Data**: Tab-separated access logs under `data/` (e.g. `log_1.tsv`, `log_2.tsv`) with columns such as `host`, `time`, `method`, `url`, `response`, `bytes`, `referer`, `useragent`.
- **Train/eval split**: Rows are sorted by `datetime`; an early **time fraction** (`data.train_time_fraction`) is **train**; the remainder is **eval**.
- **Injection** (eval only): Synthetic rows are appended with `ground_truth_anomaly = 1`; originals are `0`. Types (toggle per `configs/*.yaml`):
  - **Volume spike**: many near-duplicate requests around a tight time window for a sampled host.
  - **Rare status**: uncommon HTTP status codes (e.g. 418, 5xx family).
  - **Abnormal URL**: very long, random path segments.
  - **Timing burst**: many requests from a host with tight timestamps.
- **Reproducibility**: `seed` in YAML drives `numpy.random.Generator` for sampling and (where applicable) model randomness (e.g. Isolation Forest `random_state`).

Optional caps: `data.max_rows_per_file`, `data.max_total_rows` (seeded subsample after load).

## 5. Feature Engineering

Features are built on a **single timeline** (train + eval, sorted by time) so rolling windows see realistic host history, while **endpoint rarity** uses **train-only** URL statistics to limit leakage.

Examples:

- Temporal: `hour`, `dayofweek`, `month`.
- Request shape: `url_length`, `response_class`, `is_file`, `log_bytes`.
- Errors: `is_client_error`, `is_server_error`.
- Endpoint: `endpoint_train_count`, `endpoint_rarity_score`, `is_rare_endpoint` (threshold from config).
- Burst proxy: `same_host_minute_seq` within host + minute bucket.
- Rolling per host (configurable windows, e.g. `5min`, `1h`): request counts and mean client-error rate.

The model matrix columns are listed in `evaluation_report.json` under `data.feature_columns`.

## 6. Models

- **StandardScaler** is fit **only on train rows**; all models consume the scaled matrix.
- **Isolation Forest** (default **primary** for decisions and primary evaluation metrics): strong baseline for mixed numerical features.
- **Local Outlier Factor (novelty mode)**: optional; training subsample configurable (`max_train_samples`) for cost control.
- **One-Class SVM**: optional; also subsampled for tractability on large logs.

Primary model name is `evaluation.primary_model` in YAML and is echoed in outputs.

## 7. Evaluation (Injected Anomalies Only)

**No fake all-normal labels** are used. Metrics are **only** meaningful relative to **injected** positives:

- **Precision / recall / F1** with positive class = injected anomaly (`ground_truth_anomaly == 1`).
- **ROC-AUC** and **average precision** when both classes exist in eval.
- **Threshold sensitivity**: sweeps thresholds at train-score **percentiles** (`evaluation.threshold_percentiles`) and records PRF per point.

Two operating points are reported in `evaluation_report.json`:

- **`metrics_primary_at_investigate_threshold`**: binary prediction = `score >= t_investigate` (anything sent to triage).
- **`metrics_primary_at_alert_threshold`**: binary prediction = `score >= t_alert` (stricter).

These numbers are **not** “production accuracy” on real attacks; they measure **recovery of known synthetic injections** under a chosen unsupervised score and threshold policy.

## 8. Decision Logic

Decisions use the **primary** model’s anomaly score, where **higher = more anomalous**.

- **`ignore`**: score below `train_percentile_investigate` of **train** scores.
- **`investigate`**: score ≥ investigate percentile and < alert percentile.
- **`alert`**: score ≥ `train_percentile_alert` of **train** scores.

Thresholds are **configurable** in `decision_engine` in YAML and are recorded in `alerts_summary.json`.

## 9. Results (Honest)

After a run, expect:

| Artifact | Purpose |
|----------|---------|
| `outputs/anomaly_scores.csv` | Eval-period rows with per-model scores, primary score, and `decision`. |
| `outputs/alerts_summary.json` | Thresholds, decision counts, top scored lines (truncated URL), alerts-by-hour buckets. |
| `outputs/evaluation_report.json` | Distributions, PRF, sweep table, assumptions, feature list. |

**Expect imperfection.** Unsupervised scores rank “weird” points; many real lines are unusual yet benign. With injection rates and types in config, **precision is often modest** and **recall depends on whether injected patterns appear extreme in feature space. The value of this project is **correct methodology and system shape**, not inflated accuracy.

## 10. Limitations

- **Offline batch only**: no streaming ingestion, sharding, or real-time serving.
- **Injected anomalies are synthetic**: they approximate but do not replace red-team traffic or labeled incidents.
- **Rolling and multi-file full runs** on millions of lines can be **CPU- and memory-heavy**; use `smoke.yaml` or row caps for iteration.
- **Host-level and URL cardinality**: extremely sparse hosts or paths can dominate behavior; subsampling changes statistics.
- **Windows / joblib**: you may see loky core-count warnings; they do not invalidate results (optional: set `LOKY_MAX_CPU_COUNT`).
- **Git LFS**: `.gitattributes` may track large `*.tsv` / `*.csv`; clones need LFS where applicable.

---

**Stochasticity** is controlled by `seed` in config. **Credibility** comes from injection-backed metrics and explicit assumptions in `evaluation_report.json`.

# Distributed Session Management System with Zero-Trust Architecture

A production-grade session management platform built with Go microservices, GraphQL, and Next.js, implementing modern security practices and zero-trust principles.

## 🎯 Project Overview

This system demonstrates advanced microservices architecture, security best practices, and full-stack development skills. It implements device identity tracking, comprehensive audit logging, anomaly detection, and real-time compliance dashboards.

### Key Features

- **Device Identity Tracking**: Fingerprinting and trust scoring for every device
- **Multi-Device Session Management**: Track and manage sessions across multiple devices
- **Real-Time Security Dashboard**: Monitor active sessions, login attempts, and security alerts
- **Anomaly Detection**: Impossible travel detection, new device alerts, suspicious activity monitoring
- **Comprehensive Audit Logging**: Complete security event trail for compliance
- **Session Revocation**: Logout from all devices or specific sessions
- **Zero-Trust Architecture**: Every request verified, no implicit trust

## 🏗️ Architecture

### Microservices

```
┌─────────────┐
│   Next.js   │
│  Frontend   │
└──────┬──────┘
       │ HTTP
       ▼
┌─────────────┐
│  GraphQL    │
│  Gateway    │
└──────┬──────┘
       │ gRPC
       ├────────────┬────────────┬────────────┐
       ▼            ▼            ▼            ▼
┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐
│   Auth   │ │ Session  │ │  Audit   │ │   ...    │
│ Service  │ │ Service  │ │ Service  │ │          │
└────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ └──────────┘
     │            │            │
     └────────────┴────────────┘
                  │
                  ▼
           ┌──────────────┐
           │  PostgreSQL  │
           └──────────────┘
```

### Services

1. **Auth Service** (Port 50051)
   - User registration and authentication
   - JWT token generation and validation
   - MFA enrollment and verification
   - Password management

2. **Session Service** (Port 50052)
   - Session lifecycle management
   - Device tracking and fingerprinting
   - Multi-device session monitoring
   - Session revocation

3. **Audit Service** (Port 50053)
   - Security event logging
   - Compliance reporting
   - Activity monitoring
   - Alert generation

4. **GraphQL Gateway** (Port 8080)
   - Unified API for frontend
   - Request routing to microservices
   - Authentication middleware
   - Error handling

5. **Frontend Dashboard** (Port 3000)
   - User authentication UI
   - Session management interface
   - Real-time security monitoring
   - Device management

## 🛠️ Tech Stack

### Backend
- **Go** - High-performance, statically-typed language
- **gRPC** - Efficient inter-service communication
- **Protocol Buffers** - Type-safe service definitions
- **PostgreSQL** - Reliable relational database
- **GraphQL** - Flexible API layer

### Frontend
- **Next.js 14** - React framework with App Router
- **TypeScript** - Type-safe frontend development
- **Tailwind CSS** - Utility-first styling
- **Apollo Client** - GraphQL client

### DevOps
- **Docker** - Containerization
- **Docker Compose** - Local orchestration
- **GitHub Actions** - CI/CD pipelines

## 🚀 Getting Started

### Prerequisites

- PostgreSQL 15+ (running locally or via Docker)
- Go 1.21+
- Node.js 18+
- Protocol Buffers compiler (protoc)

### Quick Start (Local Development)

1. **Clone the repository**
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/aashiq-04/session-management-system.git
   cd session-management-system
   ```

2. **Setup Database**
   ```bash
   # Create database in PostgreSQL
   psql -U postgres
   CREATE DATABASE session_management;
   CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'admin123';
   GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE session_management TO admin;
   \c session_management
   \i database/init.sql
   \q
   ```

3. **Start Backend Services**

   **Terminal 1 - Auth Service:**
   ```bash
   cd backend/services/auth-service
   # Set environment variables (see .env file)
   go run cmd/server/main.go
   ```

   **Terminal 2 - Session Service:**
   ```bash
   cd backend/services/session-service
   # Set environment variables (see .env file)
   go run cmd/server/main.go
   ```

   **Terminal 3 - Audit Service:**
   ```bash
   cd backend/services/audit-service
   # Set environment variables (see .env file)
   go run cmd/server/main.go
   ```

   **Terminal 4 - GraphQL Gateway:**
   ```bash
   cd backend/gateway
   # Set environment variables (see .env file)
   go run cmd/server/main.go
   ```

4. **Start Frontend**
   ```bash
   cd frontend
   npm install
   npm run dev
   ```

5. **Access the application**
   - Frontend: http://localhost:3000
   - GraphQL Playground: http://localhost:8080/playground
   - Auth Service: localhost:50051 (gRPC)
   - Session Service: localhost:50052 (gRPC)
   - Audit Service: localhost:50053 (gRPC)

6. **Create your first account**
   - Navigate to http://localhost:3000
   - Click "Create one here"
   - Register with your email

### Development Setup

#### Backend Services

```bash
# Initialize Auth Service
cd backend/services/auth-service
go mod init github.com/yourusername/auth-service
go mod tidy

# Run locally
go run cmd/server/main.go
```

#### Frontend

```bash
cd frontend
npm install
npm run dev
```

## 📊 Database Schema

### Core Tables

- **users**: User credentials and profile information
- **devices**: Device fingerprints and trust scores
- **sessions**: Active and historical sessions
- **audit_logs**: Comprehensive security event logging
- **security_alerts**: Anomaly detection results
- **mfa_backup_codes**: Two-factor authentication recovery codes

## 🔒 Security Features

### Zero-Trust Implementation

1. **Authentication**: Every request requires valid JWT
2. **Device Verification**: Device fingerprinting on every login
3. **Continuous Monitoring**: Real-time session validation
4. **Audit Trail**: Complete logging of all security events

### Anomaly Detection

- **Impossible Travel**: Detects logins from geographically impossible locations
- **New Device Alerts**: Notifications for unrecognized devices
- **Suspicious Activity**: Pattern-based threat detection
- **Brute Force Protection**: Rate limiting and account lockout

### Compliance

- **Audit Logs**: Immutable security event records
- **Data Retention**: Configurable log retention policies
- **Access Reports**: Detailed activity reports
- **Privacy Controls**: GDPR-compliant data handling

## 📱 API Documentation

### GraphQL Schema

```graphql
type User {
  id: ID!
  email: String!
  fullName: String!
  mfaEnabled: Boolean!
  createdAt: String!
}

type Session {
  id: ID!
  deviceName: String
  ipAddress: String!
  location: String
  isActive: Boolean!
  createdAt: String!
  lastSeenAt: String!
}

type Query {
  me: User!
  sessions: [Session!]!
  auditLogs(limit: Int): [AuditLog!]!
  securityAlerts: [SecurityAlert!]!
}

type Mutation {
  register(email: String!, password: String!, fullName: String!): AuthPayload!
  login(email: String!, password: String!, deviceInfo: DeviceInput!): AuthPayload!
  revokeSession(sessionId: ID!): Boolean!
  revokeAllSessions: Boolean!
}
```

## 🧪 Testing

```bash
# Run backend tests
cd backend/services/auth-service
go test ./...

# Run frontend tests
cd frontend
npm test
```

## 📦 Deployment

### Production Environment Variables

```env
# Database
DB_HOST=your-db-host
DB_PORT=5432
DB_USER=your-db-user
DB_PASSWORD=your-secure-password
DB_NAME=session_management

# JWT
JWT_SECRET=your-super-secret-jwt-key-min-32-chars

# Services
AUTH_SERVICE_URL=auth-service:50051
SESSION_SERVICE_URL=session-service:50052
AUDIT_SERVICE_URL=audit-service:50053
```

Coming soon: Deployment guides for AWS, GCP, and Azure.

## 📈 Performance

- **Response Time**: <100ms for authentication
- **Throughput**: 1000+ requests/second per service
- **Database**: Indexed queries for sub-10ms lookups
- **Caching**: Redis integration for session management

This covers: neural network foundations, transformer architecture and the self-attention mechanism, training dynamics, fine-tuning strategies, and the current landscape of LLMs, vision-language models, and multimodal systems.

---

### Goal 2 — Applied Engineering

The practical dimension is structured around three concrete sub-goals, each grounded in the daily work of a software architect and test engineer.

**2a — AI-Augmented Testing & QA**
Design and build AI-assisted testing pipelines: test generation, anomaly detection in logs, intelligent test selection, and failure classification.

**2b — LLM Integration in Own Tools**
Embed LLMs into services with confidence — prompt engineering, RAG, structured outputs, tool use, evaluation, and knowing *when not to use them*.

**2c — Domain-Specific Model Adaptation**
Understand fine-tuning workflows (LoRA, instruction tuning, RLHF basics) well enough to adapt a model to a specific domain and evaluate whether it worked.

---

### Guiding Principle — Disciplined Learning Habit

This is not a goal but the principle that governs the entire project.

Build a sustainable, thinking-oriented study practice: read primary sources (papers, not just tutorials), implement key concepts from scratch at least once, and maintain a personal knowledge base that compounds over time. The goal is to learn and think — not to collect certificates or finish courses.

---

## 2. Anchor Project

**Vision-Driven GUI Test Agent**

The learning path is structured around one real-world project: building a vision-driven GUI test agent from first principles. The target application is a Windows-based diagnostic tool that interacts with engine control units via UDS diagnostics protocol.

The agent perceives the screen as pixels, reasons about what it sees, and emits mouse/keyboard actions — with no DOM or selector coupling. No XPath. No accessibility trees. Pure vision.

The project serves three roles simultaneously:
- **Motivation** — every theoretical chapter is introduced because the project needs it
- **Implementation ground** — concepts are proven by building, not by reading
- **Exam** — at each phase, something runs

| Deep Learning Concept | Role in the Project |
|---|---|
| Transformer / self-attention | Core reasoning mechanism of the VLM |
| Vision Transformer (ViT) | Screenshot perception — images as patch tokens |
| Vision-Language Models (VLMs) | The agent's perceptual and reasoning system |
| RAG + vector databases | UI element memory across test sessions |
| Agentic loop (perceive → reason → act) | The test execution architecture |
| Fine-tuning / LoRA | Adapting the VLM to the diagnostic tool's specific UI |
| AI evaluation methods | Measuring whether the agent actually works |

---

## 3. Starting Position

### 3.1 Background

- Software development education: 1997–2000 (algorithmic foundation)
- Career as Test Engineer with strong focus on test automation
- Experience: embedded software testing, safety-critical systems, aviation software verification per DO-178B (DAL A through DAL D)
- ISTQB Test Analyst certified
- Current project: testing a Windows-based diagnostic tool (UDS protocol, ECU interaction)
- Strong Python practitioner; advanced Claude Code and GitHub Copilot user
- LangChain / LangGraph — working familiarity with agentic frameworks

**Deep learning study so far:**
- Fast.AI *Practical Deep Learning for Coders* — completed through Lesson 5 (from-scratch model), with own Python implementation
- *Make Your Own Neural Network* by Tariq Rashid — read and applied

---

### 3.2 Strengths That Accelerate the Path

**Mathematical foundation is solid**
Backpropagation implemented from scratch. The training loop, gradient flow, and loss surface are understood mechanistically — not just conceptually. This is the threshold most practitioners never cross.

**Implementation velocity is high**
Deep Python experience combined with AI-assisted tooling means cognitive load can stay on *concepts*, not syntax. Ideas become code quickly.

**Agentic framework literacy**
LangChain/LangGraph familiarity means the agent architecture (perceive → reason → act) is not conceptually foreign. The gap is at the implementation internals, not the pattern.

**Testing rigour as a superpower**
DO-178B at DAL A is one of the most demanding software verification disciplines that exists. The instinct to think in terms of coverage, determinism, failure modes, and traceability is exactly what the AI industry needs — and largely lacks — when it comes to evaluating AI systems. This background will make AI evaluation work deeper than most ML engineers produce.

---

### 3.3 Knowledge Frontier

| Area | Status |
|---|---|
| Backprop, gradient descent, training loop | ✅ Solid — implemented from scratch |
| Feedforward networks, basic CNNs | ✅ Covered (Fast.AI L1–L5) |
| Transformer / self-attention mechanism | 🔶 Not yet reached |
| LLM architecture internals | 🔶 Conceptual awareness only |
| Vision-Language Models (VLMs) | ⬜ New territory |
| Fine-tuning (LoRA, PEFT) | ⬜ New territory |
| RAG architecture | 🔶 Framework-level (LangChain), not internals |
| AI system evaluation methods | 🔶 Strong intuition, formal methods new |

**The entry point in one sentence:**

> You know how a network learns. You don't yet know the self-attention mechanism — the specific computation that makes Transformers capable of context-dependent, relational reasoning across sequences.

---

## 4. Learning Path

Six phases. Each ends with something *built*.

---

### Phase 1 — The Transformer from Scratch

**Core unlock:** Self-attention mechanism, Q/K/V computation, multi-head attention, positional encoding — implemented from scratch.

**Entry point:** You built a neural net from scratch in Fast.AI Lesson 5. Andrej Karpathy's *Let's build GPT from scratch* applies exactly the same pedagogy to the Transformer. One video, ~2 hours, produces a working character-level GPT.

**Project milestone:** Read the architecture diagram of any VLM and understand every component.

**Resources:**
- Karpathy — *Let's build GPT from scratch* (YouTube) — **start here**
- Paper: *Attention is All You Need* (Vaswani et al., 2017) — read *after* the video
- Fast.AI Part 2, Lessons 12–13 (NLP section)

---

### Phase 2 — How Modern LLMs Are Built

**Core unlock:** Tokenization, embeddings, decoder-only vs. encoder architecture, pre-training objectives, the scale dimension.

**Goal:** Load GPT-2 or a small LLaMA variant, trace through every layer, and explain exactly what each one does.

**Project milestone:** Understand the *language reasoning half* of the VLM — what it does with a text instruction like *"click the reset button"*.

**Resources:**
- Hugging Face NLP Course (free)
- Karpathy — *Let's reproduce GPT-2* (follow-up video)

---

### Phase 3 — Vision-Language Models

**Core unlock:** Vision Transformer (ViT) — images as patch tokens. CLIP — aligning vision and language in a shared embedding space. LLaVA / Qwen-VL — how screenshot understanding actually works end to end.

**This is the heart of the project.** The VLM is the agent's perceptual system. Understanding it from the inside determines everything downstream.

**Project milestone:** Run a VLM locally, feed it screenshots of the diagnostic tool, and explain architecturally how it produces *"I see a warning button in the lower panel"*.

**Resources:**
- Paper: *An Image is Worth 16x16 Words* (Dosovitskiy et al.) — ViT
- Paper: *Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision* (Radford et al.) — CLIP
- Paper: *LLaVA* — focus on the architecture section
- Hands-on: run Qwen-VL or LLaVA locally via Ollama

---

### Phase 4 — The Agentic Perceive → Reason → Act Loop

**Core unlock:** Agent architecture patterns, tool use, structured outputs, state management across steps — understood at implementation depth.

**Head start:** LangGraph is the right framework. This phase deepens existing familiarity to the implementation level. Read the LangGraph source, not just the docs.

**Project milestone:** A working prototype — an agent that opens the diagnostic tool, reads the screen, and executes one deterministic test step reliably.

**Resources:**
- LangGraph documentation + source code
- Anthropic Computer Use API
- Paper: *UI-TARS* (ByteDance) — strong architecture reference, open source

---

### Phase 5 — RAG for UI Memory

**Core unlock:** Embeddings, vector databases, semantic retrieval — understood at the mechanism level, not just the LangChain API level.

**Why this matters:** The agent needs to recognize UI elements it has seen before, even when they shift slightly or change state. A persistent memory of known UI elements retrieved by semantic similarity makes the agent robust.

**Project milestone:** The agent maintains a persistent memory of the diagnostic tool's UI elements and retrieves them by semantic similarity during test execution.

**Resources:**
- Understand approximate nearest neighbour search (FAISS or HNSW) — the math behind vector search
- ChromaDB documentation
- Hugging Face — `sentence-transformers` library

---

### Phase 6 — Fine-Tuning for the Domain

**Core unlock:** LoRA, PEFT, instruction tuning — adapting a pre-trained VLM to the specific UI of the diagnostic tool.

**Why this matters:** A general VLM may struggle with domain-specific UI elements: ECU status widgets, UDS response tables, protocol-specific indicators, custom controls. Fine-tuning closes that gap with a modest amount of annotated data.

**Project milestone:** A VLM fine-tuned on annotated screenshots of the diagnostic tool, measurably outperforming the base model on the target UI elements. Evaluation methodology defined and applied — this is where the DO-178B mindset pays off.

**Resources:**
- Paper: *LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models* (Hu et al.)
- Hugging Face PEFT library
- Unsloth (efficient fine-tuning, practical tooling)
- Fast.AI Part 2 — transfer learning lessons

---

### 4.1 Phase Map

```
Phase 1 ──► Phase 2 ──► Phase 3 ──► Phase 4 ──► Phase 5 ──► Phase 6
Transformer   LLMs       VLMs       Agent       UI Memory   Fine-tune
internals    internals  internals   prototype   with RAG    for domain

◄─── Understanding the stack ────────►◄──── Building the agent ──────►

                                     ▲                              ▲
                               First thing                   Production-
                                  runs                       grade agent
```

---

### 4.2 Timing Guidance

Phases 1–3 are primarily *understanding*. Phase 4 is where something first *runs*. Do not let the theory phases expand indefinitely.

- **Phases 1–2** together: target 4–6 weeks of consistent study
- **Phase 3**: 3–4 weeks; it's dense but directly rewarding
- **Phase 4**: open-ended — this is where building starts and learning accelerates

---

*To be updated as phases are completed and the project evolves.*

# Tokenized Cross-Industry Data Exchange Platform

## Overview

A revolutionary blockchain-powered ecosystem that transforms data sharing across industries, creating a secure, transparent, and economically viable marketplace for valuable information resources.

## System Architecture

The platform is built on five core smart contracts that create a comprehensive, secure, and dynamic data exchange marketplace:

### 1. Entity Verification Contract
- **Purpose**: Authenticate and validate participating organizations
- **Key Features**:
    - Comprehensive organizational credential verification
    - Multi-level trust assessment mechanism
    - Real-time compliance monitoring
    - Dynamic organizational trust scoring
    - Secure digital identity management
    - Automated background verification
    - Cross-industry reputation tracking
    - Prevention of unauthorized network participation
    - Continuous organizational capability validation

### 2. Data Asset Registration Contract
- **Purpose**: Comprehensive recording of available information resources
- **Key Features**:
    - Detailed data asset specification logging
    - Standardized metadata management
    - Dynamic asset classification
    - Granular data type categorization
    - Intellectual property protection
    - Versioning and update tracking
    - Comprehensive data lineage recording
    - Automated data quality assessment
    - Privacy classification mechanisms

### 3. Access Control Contract
- **Purpose**: Sophisticated management of data sharing permissions
- **Key Features**:
    - Granular access rights configuration
    - Multi-level permission hierarchies
    - Time-bound access controls
    - Contextual access management
    - Consent-driven sharing mechanisms
    - Revocable data access tokens
    - Automated compliance checking
    - Privacy preservation techniques
    - Dynamic permission modification

### 4. Usage Tracking Contract
- **Purpose**: Comprehensive monitoring of data consumption
- **Key Features**:
    - Real-time data access tracking
    - Detailed usage metrics collection
    - Automated consumption logging
    - Anomaly detection systems
    - Comprehensive audit trail
    - Performance analytics
    - Predictive usage insights
    - Compliance violation detection
    - Transparent consumption reporting

### 5. Value Exchange Contract
- **Purpose**: Manage compensation for data access
- **Key Features**:
    - Tokenized payment mechanisms
    - Dynamic pricing models
    - Usage-based billing
    - Multi-currency support
    - Automated settlement
    - Escrow services
    - Micropayment capabilities
    - Royalty distribution
    - Dispute resolution framework

## Benefits

- **Monetization**: Transform data into a tradable asset
- **Collaboration**: Break down inter-industry data silos
- **Security**: Cryptographically protected information sharing
- **Transparency**: Complete visibility into data transactions
- **Efficiency**: Streamlined data marketplace
- **Innovation**: Facilitate cross-industry insights
- **Compliance**: Built-in regulatory adherence

## Technical Stack

- **Blockchain Platform**: Ethereum with Advanced Privacy Layer
- **Smart Contract Language**: Solidity
- **Privacy Technologies**: Zero-Knowledge Proofs
- **Consensus Mechanism**: Proof of Stake
- **Frontend**: React/Web3.js
- **Backend**: Node.js
- **Decentralized Storage**: IPFS with Advanced Encryption
- **AI Integration**: Machine Learning Data Valuation
- **Oracle Services**: Chainlink for External Validation

## Getting Started

- Ethereum-compatible Wallet
- Organizational Data Resources
- Node.js (v16+)

# Open-Source-IDS

# Open-Source Intrusion Detection Systems — Research & Lab Report

**Course:** CYB 623: Network Security and Defense  
**Institution:** Pace University — Seidenberg School of Computer Science and Information Systems  
**Authors:** Justin Castronuovo, Sahithi Dommeti, Mika Patel, Rayyan Baig Mirza, Andrew Peña  
**Date:** May 5, 2025

---

## Overview

This project explores the functionality and real-world deployment of four open-source Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS): **Tripwire**, **Snort**, **Suricata**, and **OSSEC**. Each tool was installed, configured, and tested in a controlled virtual lab environment using Ubuntu 20.04 VMs and Docker networks sourced from [SEED Labs](https://seedsecuritylabs.org/).

The report covers both theory and hands-on simulation — walking through detection methodologies, NIDS vs. HIDS distinctions, lab setup steps, attack simulations, and analysis of generated alerts and reports.

📄 **[View Full Report (PDF)](./IDS_Report_CYB623.pdf)**

---

## Tools Covered

| Tool | Type | Detection Method | Key Capability |
|------|------|-----------------|----------------|
| **Tripwire** | HIDS | Anomaly-based | File integrity monitoring via encrypted database snapshots |
| **Snort** | NIDS | Signature-based | Real-time packet inspection; rule-based alert engine |
| **Suricata** | NIDS/IPS | Signature + multi-mode | Multi-threaded deep packet inspection; JSON/SIEM integration |
| **OSSEC** | HIDS | Log-based / Anomaly | Real-time log analysis, severity-based alerting, active response |

---

## Lab Environments

All simulations were conducted on Ubuntu 20.04 (SEED Labs distribution) using VirtualBox and Docker.

- **Tripwire** — Single Docker container; tested file integrity detection by modifying monitored files and comparing Tripwire reports before and after
- **Snort** — Two-container Docker network (attacker + victim); simulated Nmap SYN scans and observed real-time alert generation on eth0
- **Suricata** — VirtualBox VM with bridged networking; tested built-in rule detection via a known malicious URL and created a custom HTTP content rule targeting specific keywords
- **OSSEC** — Bare Ubuntu VM (no Docker); simulated brute-force login attempts, unauthorized `su` escalation, and new user creation to trigger severity-graded alerts

---

## Key Findings

- **Tripwire** is the most accessible starting point for IDS work — straightforward setup focused on file integrity monitoring with encrypted policy and database files
- **Snort** detected ICMP pings and TCP SYN scans from the attacker container, classifying them as *Misc activity* and *Attempted Information Leak*
- **Suricata** successfully triggered alerts from both its default Emerging Threats ruleset and a custom `local.rules` file; its multi-threaded architecture makes it faster than Snort at scale
- **OSSEC** captured failed `sudo` attempts (Rule 5404, Level 10), failed `su root` logins, password changes, and a privilege escalation attempt via `usermod -aG sudo` — all logged with timestamps and severity levels in `/var/ossec/logs/alerts/alerts.log`

---

## Recommended Learning Path

For anyone getting started with open-source IDS tools:

1. **Tripwire** — Learn file integrity monitoring and how policies define violations
2. **Snort** — Move to network-based detection with a flexible rule language
3. **Suricata** — Apply similar Snort-compatible rule syntax with better performance and SIEM-ready JSON output
4. **OSSEC** — Add host-level log monitoring and active response capabilities

---

## References

- Du, W. SEED Labs: Hands-on Labs for Security Education. https://seedsecuritylabs.org/
- IBM. What is an Intrusion Detection System? https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/intrusion-detection-system

- Roesch, M. (1999). Snort – Lightweight Intrusion Detection for Networks. USENIX LISA.
- OSSEC Documentation. https://www.ossec.net/docs/

# NeuralLog Repository for the paper: [Log-based Anomaly Detection Without Log Parsing](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9678773). **Abstract**: Software systems often record important runtime information in system logs for troubleshooting purposes. There have been many studies that use log data to construct machine learning models for detecting system anomalies. Through our empirical study, we find that existing log-based anomaly detection approaches are significantly affected by log parsing errors that are introduced by 1) OOV (out-of-vocabulary) words, and 2) semantic misunderstandings. The log parsing errors could cause the loss of important information for anomaly detection. To address the limitations of existing methods, we propose NeuralLog, a novel log-based anomaly detection approach that does not require log parsing. NeuralLog extracts the semantic meaning of raw log messages and represents them as semantic vectors. These representation vectors are then used to detect anomalies through a Transformer-based classification model, which can capture the contextual information from log sequences. Our experimental results show that the proposed approach can effectively understand the semantic meaning of log messages and achieve accurate anomaly detection results. Overall, NeuralLog achieves F1-scores greater than 0.95 on four public datasets, outperforming the existing approaches. ## Framework


An overview of NeuralLog

NeuralLog consists of the following components: 1. **Preprocessing**: Special characters and numbers are removed from log messages. 2. **Neural Representation**: Semantic vectors are extracted from log messages using BERT. 3. **Transformer-based Classification**: A transformer-based classification model containing Positional Encoding and Transformer Encoder is applied to detect anomalies. SmartLogGuard — Real-time Log Anomaly Detection Platform

> A production-inspired log monitoring platform that ingests application logs via Apache Kafka, detects anomalies using Machine Learning (Isolation Forest), and delivers real-time alerts to engineers through a live WebSocket dashboard — before users even notice a problem.

---

---

## 💡 What Problem Does It Solve?

Traditional log monitoring systems are **reactive** — engineers find out about problems **after** users are already impacted. SmartLogGuard solves this by:

| Problem | Solution |
|---|---|
| Too many logs to monitor manually | Kafka streams logs in real-time, ML auto-detects anomalies |
| Rule-based alerts miss unknown failures | Isolation Forest detects novel patterns without labeled data |
| Dashboards require manual refresh | WebSocket pushes alerts instantly — zero polling |
| Single server log processor bottleneck | Kafka decouples producers/consumers, scales horizontally |
| Slow incident response (minutes to hours) | Anomaly detected and alerted within seconds |

---

 System Architecture

```
Log Simulator (Python)
        ↓
POST /api/logs/send
        ↓
Spring Boot (LogProducer)
        ↓
Apache Kafka [raw-logs topic]
        ↓
Spring Boot (LogConsumer)
        ↓         ↓
   MySQL DB    HTTP POST → Python FastAPI (/predict)
   (save log)        ↓
               Isolation Forest ML Model
                      ↓
               Anomaly Score (0.0 - 1.0)
                      ↓
              if score > 0.7 → ANOMALY!
                      ↓
              Save Alert → MySQL
              Cache Stats → Redis
              Push Alert → WebSocket
                      ↓
              React Dashboard (live update)
```

---

 Tech Stack

### Backend — Spring Boot (Java)
| Technology | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Spring Boot 3.x | Core backend framework |
| Apache Kafka | Real-time log streaming (producer + consumer) |
| Spring WebSocket (STOMP) | Push live alerts to React dashboard |
| Spring Data JPA | MySQL ORM |
| Spring Data Redis | Cache recent logs and alerts |
| Spring Security | CORS configuration |
| WebFlux (WebClient) | HTTP calls to Python ML service |
| Lombok | Boilerplate reduction |
| SLF4J | Logging throughout pipeline |

### ML Service — Python
| Technology | Purpose |
|---|---|
| FastAPI | REST API framework (exposes /predict endpoint) |
| Isolation Forest (scikit-learn) | Unsupervised anomaly detection ML model |
| Pydantic | Request/response data validation |
| NumPy | Feature array preparation |
| joblib | Save and load trained ML model |
| kafka-python | Optional direct Kafka consumer |
| Uvicorn | ASGI server to run FastAPI |

### Frontend — React
| Technology | Purpose |
|---|---|
| React + Vite | Frontend framework |
| Tailwind CSS | Styling |
| Redux Toolkit | Global state management |
| @stomp/stompjs + SockJS | WebSocket client for live alerts |
| Axios | HTTP calls to Spring Boot REST API |
| Recharts | Anomaly score timeline chart |
| Roboto + Roboto Mono | Typography |

### Infrastructure
| Technology | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Docker + Docker Compose | Containerize Kafka, Zookeeper, Redis |
| MySQL | Persistent storage for logs and alerts |
| Redis | Cache frequently accessed data (10min TTL) |
| Apache Kafka + Zookeeper | Message broker for log streaming |

---

## 🔍 How It Works — Step by Step

**Step 1 — Log Generation**
A Python simulator generates realistic log events (85% normal, 15% anomalous) and sends them via HTTP POST to Spring Boot every 0.5–1.5 seconds.

**Step 2 — Kafka Streaming**
Spring Boot's `LogProducer` publishes each log as a JSON message to the `raw-logs` Kafka topic. Kafka acts as a durable, ordered queue — decoupling log producers from consumers.

**Step 3 — Log Consumption**
`LogConsumer` (annotated with `@KafkaListener`) automatically picks up each message the moment it arrives — no polling needed.

**Step 4 — Persistence**
`LogService` saves each log entry to MySQL via JPA (`log_entries` table) for audit trail and historical queries.

**Step 5 — ML Scoring**
`MLClientService` sends extracted features (error rate, response time, error count, warn count, log volume) via HTTP POST to the Python FastAPI `/predict` endpoint using `WebClient`.

**Step 6 — Isolation Forest Prediction**
The pre-trained Isolation Forest model scores the features:
- Score > 0.7 → **Anomaly detected**
- Score ≤ 0.7 → Normal log

Isolation Forest is unsupervised — no labeled data needed. It learns what "normal" looks like and flags deviations automatically.

**Step 7 — Alert Creation**
If anomaly detected:
- Score ≥ 0.85 → **HIGH** severity
- Score 0.7–0.84 → **MEDIUM** severity
- Alert saved to MySQL (`anomaly_alerts` table)
- Recent alerts cache evicted from Redis
- Alert pushed to React via WebSocket

**Step 8 — Live Dashboard Update**
React's `useWebSocket` hook (STOMP over SockJS) receives the alert instantly. Dashboard updates with no refresh — live log stream, anomaly alerts panel, and score timeline chart all update in real time.

---

## 🤖 Why Isolation Forest?

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Type | Unsupervised ML — no labeled data needed |
| How it works | Anomalies are isolated in fewer tree splits than normal points |
| Features used | error_rate, avg_response_time, error_count, warn_count, log_volume |
| Training data | 900 synthetic normal samples + 100 anomalous samples |
| Contamination | 0.1 (expects ~10% anomalies) |
| Output | Score 0.0–1.0 (higher = more anomalous) |
| Threshold | Score > 0.7 triggers alert |

---

---

## ⚙️ Local Setup

### Prerequisites
- Java 17+
- Maven
- Python 3.11+

### Step 1 — Start Infrastructure
```bash
docker-compose up -d
```


- **Live Anomaly Alerts** — Real-time alert panel with severity badge, anomaly score progress bar, description

---

| Python FastAPI for ML | Best ML ecosystem (scikit-learn), clean REST interface |

It transforms traditional IT operations into an intelligent, automated workflow — from monitoring and alerting to root-cause analysis and ticket generation — all running **100% on-premise** with zero cloud dependencies. MCP v7 orchestrates **35 Docker containers** across **5 isolated networks**, organized into functional stacks behind a single Nginx reverse proxy. The local AI stack (Ollama + LangChain + pgvector) analyzes events in real-time, searches a knowledge base of past incidents, and generates professional, actionable tickets automatically. ``` Zabbix Alert ┌──────────────────────┐ CrowdSec Finding ─→ n8n Workflow ─→ │ AI Gateway (FastAPI) │ Loki Anomaly └──────────┬───────────┘ │ ┌───────────▼───────────┐ │ LangChain Worker │ │ 1. complete 7-step pipeline for each alert: ``` 1. JOB INTAKE Redis BRPOP from mcp:queue:analyze ↓ 2. RAG SEARCH Embed description → pgvector similarity search (top_k=5, threshold=0.7) → Returns similar past incidents from last 90 days ↓ 3. PROMPT ASSEMBLY Load template from config/ai/prompts/alert-analysis.txt → Fill: {alert_type}, {source}, {hostname}, {severity}, {description}, {metrics}, {logs}, {crowdsec_alerts}, {rag_results} ↓ 4. LLM ANALYSIS LiteLLM (http://litellm:4000) → OpenAI-compatible API → Fallback: Ollama direct (http://ollama:11434) → Returns structured JSON: root_cause, impact, actions, confidence ↓ 5. TICKET CREATION If severity ≥ high OR confidence = High: → POST http://zammad-rails:3000/api/v1/tickets → Structured ticket with AI analysis, priority, recommended actions ↓ 6. NOTIFICATION ntfy push to mcp-alerts channel → Severity → Priority mapping (Critical=5, High=4, Medium=3, Low=2) ↓ 7. FEEDBACK LOOP Embed analysis summary → store in pgvector → Future RAG searches will find this incident → Audit log entry with confidence score, model used, processing time ``` ### AI Configuration ```yaml # config/ai/models.yml — Model routing via LiteLLM primary_model: mistral:7b-instruct-v0.3-q4_K_M # Analysis, tickets, root-cause fallback_model: llama3:8b-instruct-q4_K_M # Automatic failover embedding_model: nomic-embed-text # 768-dim vectors for RAG # config/ai/rag-config.yml — RAG pipeline tuning chunk_size: 512 # Document chunking for ingestion chunk_overlap: 50 # Overlap between chunks top_k: 5 # Similar documents per query similarity_threshold: 0.7 # Minimum cosine similarity max_age_days: 90 # RAG search window max_concurrent_jobs: 3 # Parallel analysis jobs job_timeout: 120s # Per-job timeout ``` --- ## Smart Ticketing Every AI-generated ticket follows a structured format optimized for MSP workflows. The ticket content is produced by a German-language prompt template: | Field | Content | Source | |-------|---------|--------| | `ticket_title` | Concise incident title | AI-generated | | `root_cause` | Why it happened — 1–2 sentences | LLM correlation | | `impact` | Gering / Mittel / Hoch / Kritisch | LLM assessment | | `affected_services` | Which services/clients are impacted | Service map analysis | | `immediate_action` | Concrete steps to fix now | AI + RAG knowledge base | | `long_term_solution` | Prevention strategy | AI + best practices | | `confidence` | High / Medium / Low with reasoning | Model self-assessment | | `ticket_priority` | 1_low / 2_normal / 3_high / 4_urgent | Mapped from impact + confidence | ### Confidence-Based Routing | Confidence | Severity | Action | |------------|----------|--------| | **High** + High/Critical severity | Automatic | Ticket created + assigned + ntfy push | | **Medium** | Automatic | Ticket created as draft + ntfy push | | **Low** | Alert only | ntfy notification, no ticket — human takes over | ### Example: Printer Monitoring **Scenario:** Network printer `192.168.1.50` reports paper jam 1. **Zabbix** detects SNMP trap → status change 2. **n8n** workflow triggered → enriches alert with metrics, toner status, error history 3. **AI Gateway** receives alert → queues in Redis, deduplication check (15 min window) 4. **LangChain Worker** pops job → RAG finds 3 similar printer incidents from past 90 days 5. **Ollama/Mistral** analyzes → "Recurring paper jam in tray 2, feed roller likely worn" 6. **Zammad** ticket created: `[DRUCKER] HP LaserJet 402 — Recurring Paper Jam Tray 2` 7. **ntfy** push sent to responsible technician (priority 3 = medium) 8. **pgvector** stores analysis embedding → future similar incidents find this solution --- ## # 🛰️ Satellite Telemetry Anomaly Detection System  
### Real-Time Streaming | Machine Learning | Mission Control Dashboard

A **production-grade real-time anomaly detection system** for satellite telemetry streams, built using deep learning and a mission-control-style dashboard.  
This system simulates live satellite data streams, detects anomalies using a trained autoencoder model, and provides real-time visualization and analytics for operators.

> 🚀 Designed with **space missions, ground stations, and ISRO-style telemetry monitoring** in mind.

---

## 🔍 Problem Statement

Satellite missions generate **continuous, high-dimensional telemetry data** from multiple onboard subsystems.  
Manual monitoring is:
- Error-prone  
- Not scalable  
- Unable to react quickly to subtle or early anomalies  

Early detection of anomalies is **critical** to:
- Prevent subsystem failures  
- Reduce mission risk  
- Enable timely corrective actions  

---

## 💡 Solution Overview

This project delivers a **real-time telemetry anomaly detection platform** that:

- Simulates live satellite telemetry streams
- Uses a **deep learning autoencoder** for multivariate anomaly detection
- Applies **sliding-window inference** for temporal context
- Classifies anomaly severity in real time
- Visualizes telemetry and anomalies via a **mission-control dashboard**

---

## ✨ Key Features

### 🔴 Real-Time Streaming
- Row-by-row telemetry streaming from CSV
- Adjustable streaming speed (0.05–1.0 sec per row)
- Pause, Resume, Replay controls
- Progress tracking and looped replay

### 🧠 Machine Learning Engine
- Pre-trained **LSTM Autoencoder**
- Multivariate reconstruction error (MSE)
- MinMax normalization
- Threshold-based anomaly decisioning

### ⚠️ Anomaly Detection & Severity
- Binary detection: NORMAL / ANOMALY
- Severity levels:
  - LOW
  - MEDIUM
  - HIGH
- Error-to-threshold ratio based classification

### 📊 Mission Control Dashboard
- Live telemetry table (20 channels)
- Real-time reconstruction error graph
- Threshold overlay and anomaly markers
- Status indicators with color coding
- Real-time metrics and statistics

### 📈 Analytics & Logs
- Anomaly count and severity distribution
- Anomaly density and intervals
- Recent anomaly log
- Downloadable anomaly report (CSV)

---

Businesses and users benefit from clean datasets, improved efficiency, and repeatable workflows. ### Automated Mobile Conversation Analytics - Captures conversation transcript elements consistently across multiple sessions and devices. - Applies NLP-driven tagging and scoring logic for message timing, tone classification, and engagement metrics. - Supports both local and remote device execution for large-scale data pipelines. - Minimizes human error and increases throughput for behavioral research and UX teams. - Built with modular components that can be integrated into larger automation systems. ## # Cybersecurity Threat Detection with AI ML-powered security system: network intrusion detection with autoencoders, log anomaly detection with transformers, malware classification with gradient-boosted trees, and NLP-based threat intelligence extraction from CVE reports and security advisories. ## Theory & Background ### The Detection Problem A mid-size enterprise network generates millions of events per day — NetFlow records, system logs, DNS queries, authentication attempts. A security operations center (SOC) analyst can realistically triage maybe 50 alerts per shift. If even 0.5% of events are flagged, that's thousands of alerts drowning the real threats in noise. The fundamental challenge is finding the rare malicious signal in overwhelming benign traffic, where false positive rates must stay below roughly 0.1% to be operationally useful. No single detector catches everything. A port scan looks normal in NetFlow if you only check packet sizes. A credential-stuffing attack looks normal in logs if you only check individual entries. Malware can evade static signatures by repacking. This is why layered defense matters — each detector covers a different attack surface, and their combined signal is far stronger than any one alone. This project implements four complementary detection approaches that together form a defense-in-depth pipeline: 1. **Reconstruction-based anomaly detection** for network traffic (autoencoders) 2. **Sequence modeling** for log anomalies (transformers) 3. **Supervised classification** for malware (gradient-boosted trees on PE features) 4. **NLP extraction** for threat intelligence (regex NER + IOC extraction) ### Detection Pipeline Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph Sources["Data Sources"] NF[NetFlow Records] SL[System Logs] PE[PE Executables] CVE[CVE Reports /
Security Advisories] end subgraph Features["Feature Engineering"] NF --> FE1[Flow Statistics
Byte Ratios, Packet Rates] SL --> FE2[Log Tokenization
Template Extraction] PE --> FE3[PE Header Features
Section Entropy, Imports] CVE --> FE4[Regex NER
IOC Pattern Matching] end subgraph Models["Detection Models"] FE1 --> M1[Autoencoder
Reconstruction Anomaly] FE2 --> M2[Transformer
Sequence Perplexity] FE3 --> M3[XGBoost
Malware Classifier] FE4 --> M4[IOC Extractor
Entity Recognition] end subgraph Scoring["Scoring & Alerting"] M1 --> SC[Weighted Threat Scorer] M2 --> SC M3 --> SC M4 --> TI[Threat Intel DB] SC --> AL[Alert Engine
Threshold + Priority] AL --> |LOW / MED / HIGH / CRITICAL| OUT[SOC Dashboard] end ``` ### Anomaly Detection via Autoencoders #### Intuition Imagine you train a photocopier that only ever sees pictures of cats. When you feed it a cat, the copy is nearly perfect. When you feed it a dog, the copy comes out garbled — the machine doesn't know how to reproduce something it's never seen. An autoencoder works the same way: trained only on normal network traffic, it reconstructs benign patterns faithfully but produces high error on anything anomalous. This is powerful because you never need labeled attack data for training. You only need a clean baseline of normal traffic, which is far easier to obtain than a comprehensive catalog of every possible attack. #### Architecture The autoencoder compresses a NetFlow feature vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ through an encoder $f$ into a low-dimensional latent representation $z \in \mathbb{R}^k$ (where $k \ll d$), then reconstructs it through a decoder $g$. The bottleneck forces the network to learn a compact representation of "normal." The implementation uses a multi-layer encoder ($d \to 64 \to 32 \to 16$) with batch normalization and dropout at each layer, mirrored by a symmetric decoder ($16 \to 32 \to 64 \to d$). Training minimizes the mean squared reconstruction error over normal traffic only: ```math \mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \| x_i - g(f(x_i)) \|^2 ``` This loss measures how well the autoencoder can reproduce each input. On normal data, the loss converges to a small value. On anomalous data the model has never seen, the reconstruction is poor and the error spikes. At inference, the anomaly score for a new observation is simply its per-sample reconstruction error: ```math \text{score}(x) = \| x - g(f(x)) \|^2 ``` An alert fires when $\text{score}(x) > \tau$, where the threshold $\tau$ is calibrated on held-out clean data. #### Threshold Calibration Choosing $\tau$ is the critical operational decision. Set it too low and analysts drown in false alarms; set it too high and real attacks slip through. The threshold is set at a target false positive rate (FPR) using the empirical distribution of reconstruction errors on clean validation data: ```math \tau = \text{Quantile}_{1 - \text{FPR}}(\{\text{score}(x_i) : x_i \in \mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}\}) ``` For example, $\tau$ at the 99.9th percentile corresponds to a 0.1% FPR — roughly 1 false alarm per 1000 flows. This adapts automatically to each deployment's traffic distribution, unlike a fixed threshold. #### Feature Engineering Raw NetFlow records are transformed into a feature vector with engineered ratios and rates that capture attack signatures: | Feature | What it captures | |---------|-----------------| | `bytes_ratio` = $\frac{\text{sent}}{\text{recv} + 1}$ | Exfiltration (high ratio) vs. download (low ratio) | | `packets_per_second` | DDoS bursts (extremely high) vs. normal browsing | | `avg_packet_size` | Port scans (tiny packets) vs. file transfers (large) | | `log_bytes_sent` | Log-scaled to handle the heavy-tailed distribution | | `is_well_known_dst` | Whether the destination port is < 1024 | All features are standardized with `StandardScaler` before feeding to the autoencoder, since reconstruction error is sensitive to feature scale. ### Log Anomaly Detection with Transformers #### Intuition System logs follow predictable patterns: a successful SSH login produces the same sequence of log templates every time. An attacker's activity — failed logins from unusual IPs, privilege escalation commands, unexpected service restarts — breaks these patterns. If you train a language model on normal log sequences, anomalous sequences will have high perplexity (the model is "surprised" by what it sees). This is the same principle behind how your phone's keyboard predicts the next word. If you type something completely unexpected, the prediction confidence drops. We exploit that drop in confidence as an anomaly signal. #### Log Tokenization Raw logs are messy — they contain timestamps, IP addresses, file paths, and process IDs that change every time. Feeding raw text directly would create an enormous vocabulary where the model memorizes specific IPs instead of learning structural patterns. The `LogTokenizer` solves this with drain-style template extraction: variable parts are replaced with typed placeholders before tokenization. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Raw as Raw Log Line participant Norm as Normalizer participant Tok as Tokenizer participant Model as Transformer Raw->>Norm: "Failed login from 192.168.1.42 port 22" Norm->>Norm: Replace IP → Norm->>Norm: Replace numbers → Norm->>Tok: "failed login from port " Tok->>Tok: Split + vocabulary lookup Tok->>Model: [2, 47, 103, 5, 88, 4, 3] Note over Model: BOS + tokens + EOS ``` This normalization reduces vocabulary size by orders of magnitude (from millions of unique strings to ~5000 templates) while preserving the structural patterns that distinguish normal from anomalous sequences. #### Model Architecture The `LogTransformer` is a causal transformer language model trained with next-token prediction. It uses 3 transformer encoder layers with 4 attention heads and a 128-dimensional embedding, plus learned positional embeddings for sequences up to 128 tokens. The training objective is the standard autoregressive cross-entropy loss: ```math \mathcal{L}_{\text{log}} = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log P_\theta(x_t \mid x_1, \ldots, x_{t-1}) ``` where $x_t$ is the log token at position $t$, and $P_\theta$ is the model's predicted probability given all preceding tokens. The model learns that after "sshd: accepted publickey for" the next token is almost certainly a username template — if it sees something wildly different, the probability drops. At inference, the anomaly score is the perplexity of the observed sequence: ```math \text{Perplexity}(x_{1:T}) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log P_\theta(x_t \mid x_{ Ingested: Raw event arrives Ingested --> FeatureExtracted: Feature engineering FeatureExtracted --> Scored: Model inference Scored --> Suppressed: score < threshold Scored --> AlertGenerated: score ≥ threshold AlertGenerated --> Classified: Assign threat level Classified --> LOW: score < 0.4 Classified --> MEDIUM: 0.4 ≤ score < 0.6 Classified --> HIGH: 0.6 ≤ score < 0.8 Classified --> CRITICAL: score ≥ 0.8 CRITICAL --> Escalated: Immediate response HIGH --> Triaged: SOC analyst review MEDIUM --> Queued: Batch review LOW --> Logged: Record only Suppressed --> [*] Escalated --> [*] Triaged --> [*] Queued --> [*] Logged --> [*] ``` ### Scoring and Fusion The `ThreatScorer` combines normalized scores from all four detectors into a single threat score using a weighted average: ```math S_{\text{overall}} = w_{\text{ids}} \cdot s_{\text{ids}} + w_{\text{log}} \cdot s_{\text{log}} + w_{\text{mal}} \cdot s_{\text{mal}} + w_{\text{ti}} \cdot s_{\text{ti}} ``` where each $s_i \in [0, 1]$ is a detector's normalized score and the default weights are $w_{\text{ids}} = 0.3$, $w_{\text{log}} = 0.25$, $w_{\text{mal}} = 0.25$, $w_{\text{ti}} = 0.2$. Network intrusion gets the highest weight because it covers the broadest attack surface. Weights are tunable per-environment based on historical alert quality. Individual component alerts fire independently when any single detector exceeds the medium threshold ($s_i \geq 0.4$), so a high-confidence malware detection triggers an alert even if the other detectors are quiet. ### Evaluation: Precision-Recall at Low FPR In security, the cost of errors is asymmetric. A false negative (missed attack) can mean a breach. A false positive (false alarm) wastes analyst time and causes alert fatigue. The right metric depends on which cost dominates. The $F_\beta$ score lets you tune this tradeoff: ```math F_\beta = (1 + \beta^2) \cdot \frac{\text{Precision} \cdot \text{Recall}}{\beta^2 \cdot \text{Precision} + \text{Recall}} ``` - $\beta = 1$: Equal weight to precision and recall (standard $F_1$) - $\beta = 2$: Recall-weighted — missing an attack is $4\times$ worse than a false alarm - $\beta = 0.5$: Precision-weighted — false alarms are $4\times$ worse than missed attacks For intrusion detection, $\beta = 2$ is standard because missing an active breach is catastrophic. For malware scanning at scale (millions of files), $\beta = 0.5$ may be appropriate to keep false positive volume manageable. **Operational targets:** - Precision ≥ 0.85 at 0.1% FPR for network intrusion - Recall ≥ 0.95 for known malware families - $F_1$ ≥ 0.90 for IOC entity extraction ### Pipeline Processing Timeline ```mermaid gantt title Event Processing Pipeline dateFormat X axisFormat %s section Network IDS NetFlow ingestion :0, 1 Feature engineering :1, 2 Autoencoder inference :2, 3 Threshold check :3, 4 section Log Anomaly Log collection :0, 1 Template tokenization :1, 3 Transformer inference :3, 5 Perplexity scoring :5, 6 section Malware PE submission :0, 1 Static feature extract:1, 2 XGBoost classify :2, 3 section Threat Intel Report ingestion :0, 2 IOC extraction :2, 4 NER entity tagging :4, 6 DB insertion :6, 7 section Fusion Score aggregation :6, 7 Alert generation :7, 8 SOC notification :8, 9 ``` ### Tradeoffs and Alternatives | Decision | Choice | Alternative | Why this choice | |----------|--------|-------------|-----------------| | IDS model | Autoencoder | Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM | Scales to high-dimensional features; learns nonlinear boundaries; threshold is interpretable | | Log model | Causal Transformer | LSTM, DeepLog (LSTM-based) | Better at capturing long-range dependencies in log sequences; parallelizable training | | Malware model | XGBoost | Deep neural network, Random Forest | Best performance on tabular data with ~12 features; built-in feature importance; trains in seconds | | NER approach | Rule-based regex | Fine-tuned SecBERT | Zero training data required; deterministic; covers known taxonomies (MITRE ATT&CK, CVE). Trade: misses novel entity names | | Score fusion | Weighted average | Learned meta-classifier | Transparent, tunable per-environment; no additional training data needed. Trade: can't learn nonlinear interactions between detectors | | Threshold | Percentile-based on clean data | Fixed threshold | Adapts to each deployment's traffic distribution automatically | **When autoencoders fail**: Slow-and-low attacks that mimic normal traffic patterns (e.g., exfiltrating small amounts of data over weeks) produce low reconstruction error because they stay within the learned distribution. These require session-level or graph-based detection approaches. **When log transformers fail**: If the training corpus doesn't cover a legitimate but rare log pattern (e.g., annual certificate rotation), the model flags it as anomalous. Regular retraining on updated baselines mitigates this. ### Key References - Mirsky et al., "Kitsune: An Ensemble of Autoencoders for Online Network Intrusion Detection" (2018) — [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.09089) - Du et al., "DeepLog: Anomaly Detection and Diagnosis from System Logs through Deep Learning" (2017) — [ACM](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3133956.3134015) - Raff et al., "Malware Detection by Eating a Whole EXE" (2018) — [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.09435) - Lim et al., "Mal2Vec: Malware Representation Learning with Word2Vec" (2019) - Bridges et al., "A Survey of Intrusion Detection Systems Leveraging Host Data" (2019) — [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.01110) - Chen & Guestrin, "XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System" (2016) — [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.02754) ## Real-World Applications AI-driven threat detection allows security teams to monitor millions of events per day and surface genuine threats without drowning analysts in false alarms. Organizations that deploy these systems detect breaches faster, reduce the manual workload on security operations centers, and maintain compliance with regulatory frameworks that mandate continuous monitoring. | Industry | Use Case | Impact | |----------|----------|--------| | Financial Services | Real-time network anomaly detection across trading infrastructure and customer-facing banking systems | Faster identification of unauthorized access and data exfiltration attempts, reducing mean time to detect from days to minutes | | Healthcare | Log anomaly detection on electronic health record systems and connected medical devices to flag unauthorized access patterns | Supports HIPAA compliance by providing continuous audit trails and automated alerting on suspicious access to patient data | | Government & Defense | Automated threat intelligence extraction from CVE advisories and security bulletins, feeding structured IOCs into defensive systems | Analysts spend less time reading reports and more time acting — structured threat feeds enable faster patch prioritization and blocking | | Managed Security Providers | Multi-tenant malware classification and alert scoring across hundreds of client environments with a single detection pipeline | Scales analyst capacity across a growing client base without proportional headcount increases, improving margins on managed services | | Critical Infrastructure | Layered detection combining network intrusion, log anomaly, and threat intel to protect SCADA and industrial control systems | Defense-in-depth coverage where no single detector is sufficient — combined scoring catches multi-stage attacks that evade individual sensors | ## Project Structure ``` ├── src/ │ ├── intrusion/ │ │ ├── autoencoder.py # Anomaly autoencoder (encoder → bottleneck → decoder) │ │ ├── features.py # NetFlow feature engineering + synthetic data gen │ │ └── train.py # Training loop with threshold calibration │ ├── log_anomaly/ │ │ ├── model.py # Causal transformer for log sequence modeling │ │ ├── tokenizer.py # Drain-style log template tokenization │ │ └── train.py # Training loop with perplexity evaluation │ ├── malware/ │ │ ├── classifier.py # XGBoost malware classifier + synthetic PE features │ │ └── features.py # PE file static feature extraction │ ├── threat_intel/ │ │ ├── ner_model.py # Rule-based NER for threat actors, malware, techniques │ │ └── ioc_extractor.py # IOC extraction (IPs, hashes, CVEs, domains) │ └── pipeline/ │ └── scorer.py # Weighted threat scorer + alert engine ├── data/ │ └── sample/ # Sample datasets ├── configs/ ├── notebooks/ │ └── walkthrough.ipynb ├── requirements.txt └── README.md ``` ## Quick Start ```bash pip install -r requirements.txt # Train intrusion detection autoencoder python -m src.intrusion.train --data data/sample/netflow.csv # Train log anomaly transformer python -m src.log_anomaly.train --data data/sample/logs.txt # Classify PE files for malware python -m src.malware.classifier # Extract IOCs from threat reports python -m src.threat_intel.ioc_extractor --input data/sample/cve_reports.json # Run NER on a security advisory python -m src.threat_intel.ner_model # Run real-time scoring pipeline python -m src.pipeline.scorer --config configs/scorer.yaml ``` ## Implementation Details ### What makes this non-trivial - **Threshold calibration**: The autoencoder anomaly threshold is set at a target FPR on held-out clean data using percentile-based calibration, not a fixed value — this adapts to the traffic distribution of each deployment - **Log tokenization**: Raw logs are parsed into structured templates by replacing IPs, paths, hex values, and numbers with typed placeholders (``, ``, ``, ``), reducing vocabulary from millions of unique strings to ~5000 templates - **Weighted score fusion**: The real-time scorer combines anomaly scores from four detectors using configurable weighted aggregation, with independent per-component alerting so a high-confidence single-detector signal isn't diluted by quiet detectors - **PE feature entropy**: Malware classification uses section-level entropy as a key discriminator — packed or encrypted malware sections have near-maximum entropy (~7.2 bits/byte) compared to normal code sections (~5.5), and the XGBoost model surfaces this automatically via feature importance - **IOC normalization**: Extracted indicators are deduplicated, false-positive filtered (removing `127.0.0.1`, `example.com`), and enriched with surrounding context for analyst review - **Overlap-aware NER**: The entity extractor processes patterns in priority order and tracks extracted spans to prevent overlapping entity annotations, ensuring each text span maps to exactly one entity type
